A REST API lets other programs, like a web page or a mobile app, read and change your data over HTTP. Spring Boot is the most used way to build one in Java. We'll build a small book API in five short classes, with a real database, input validation and clear error messages, then test it.

Here's what it will do:

Method URL Does Answers
GET /api/books List books, by author or all 200 and a list
GET /api/books/{id} Get one book 200, or 404
POST /api/books Add a book 201, or 400
PUT /api/books/{id} Replace a book 200, 400 or 404
DELETE /api/books/{id} Delete a book 204, or 404

Create the Project

Go to start.spring.io, choose Maven, Java 21 and the latest Spring Boot 4 version, and add these dependencies:

  • Spring Web: the web server and controllers (the spring-boot-starter-webmvc starter, called spring-boot-starter-web before Spring Boot 4).
  • Spring Data JPA: saving Java objects in a database.
  • Validation: checking the input.
  • H2 Database: a small database that runs in memory, so there's nothing to install.

Download the project, open it in your editor, and run the class with the main method. Spring Boot starts a web server on port 8080.

The app is split into layers, each with one job:

HTTP request → Controller → Service → Repository → Database
               (web)        (rules)   (data access)

The Entity: What We Store

An entity is a class that JPA saves as a row in a table. @Id marks the primary key, and @GeneratedValue lets the database pick it.

@Entity
public class Book {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;
    private String title;
    private String author;
    private int pages;

    protected Book() {} // for JPA

    public Book(String title, String author, int pages) {
        this.title = title;
        this.author = author;
        this.pages = pages;
    }

    public Long getId() { return id; }
    public String getTitle() { return title; }
    public String getAuthor() { return author; }
    public int getPages() { return pages; }

    public void update(String title, String author, int pages) {
        this.title = title;
        this.author = author;
        this.pages = pages;
    }
}

JPA needs the empty constructor to create objects from rows. With H2, Spring Boot creates the book table for you when the app starts.

Watch out for field names that are reserved words in SQL. A field named year, order or user makes H2 fail with "Syntax error in SQL statement" when it creates the table. Pick another name, like publishedYear.

The Repository: Talking to the Database

You don't write the database code. Declare an interface that extends JpaRepository, and Spring Data writes the class for you, with save, findById, findAll, deleteById and more:

public interface BookRepository extends JpaRepository<Book, Long> {
    List<Book> findByAuthorIgnoreCase(String author);
}

Spring Data even reads method names: findByAuthorIgnoreCase becomes a query like WHERE lower(author) = lower(?).

Requests and Responses: Records, Not the Entity

Don't send the entity itself in and out of the API. Use small records for what the API receives and returns. Then you can change the database without breaking the apps that use your API, and a client can't set fields it shouldn't, like id.

public record BookRequest(
    @NotBlank String title,
    @NotBlank String author,
    @Positive int pages) {}

public record BookResponse(Long id, String title, String author, int pages) {
    static BookResponse from(Book book) {
        return new BookResponse(book.getId(), book.getTitle(), book.getAuthor(), book.getPages());
    }
}

@NotBlank and @Positive are validation rules. They're checked in the controller, as you'll see.

The Service: The Rules

The service holds what your app does, apart from HTTP. Spring creates it and passes it the repository through the constructor: that's dependency injection.

@Service
public class BookService {
    private final BookRepository repository;

    public BookService(BookRepository repository) {
        this.repository = repository;
    }

    public List<BookResponse> findAll(String author) {
        List<Book> books = author == null
            ? repository.findAll()
            : repository.findByAuthorIgnoreCase(author);
        return books.stream().map(BookResponse::from).toList();
    }

    public BookResponse findById(Long id) {
        return repository.findById(id)
            .map(BookResponse::from)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new BookNotFoundException(id));
    }

    public BookResponse create(BookRequest request) {
        Book book = new Book(request.title(), request.author(), request.pages());
        return BookResponse.from(repository.save(book));
    }

    @Transactional
    public BookResponse update(Long id, BookRequest request) {
        Book book = repository.findById(id)
            .orElseThrow(() -> new BookNotFoundException(id));
        book.update(request.title(), request.author(), request.pages());
        return BookResponse.from(book);
    }

    public void delete(Long id) {
        if (!repository.existsById(id)) {
            throw new BookNotFoundException(id);
        }
        repository.deleteById(id);
    }
}

update never calls save. Inside a @Transactional method, JPA watches the objects it loaded and writes their changes to the database when the method ends.

The exception is a plain class:

public class BookNotFoundException extends RuntimeException {
    public BookNotFoundException(Long id) {
        super("No book with id " + id);
    }
}

The Controller: The HTTP Part

The controller turns HTTP requests into service calls. @RestController means every method's return value is sent back as JSON.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/books")
public class BookController {
    private final BookService service;

    public BookController(BookService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }

    @GetMapping
    public List<BookResponse> list(@RequestParam(required = false) String author) {
        return service.findAll(author);
    }

    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public BookResponse get(@PathVariable Long id) {
        return service.findById(id);
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<BookResponse> create(@Valid @RequestBody BookRequest request) {
        BookResponse created = service.create(request);
        return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/api/books/" + created.id())).body(created);
    }

    @PutMapping("/{id}")
    public BookResponse update(@PathVariable Long id, @Valid @RequestBody BookRequest request) {
        return service.update(id, request);
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
    @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
    public void delete(@PathVariable Long id) {
        service.delete(id);
    }
}
  • @PathVariable reads {id} from the URL. @RequestParam reads ?author=….
  • @RequestBody turns the JSON body into a BookRequest, and @Valid checks its rules before your method runs.
  • Creating answers 201 Created with a Location header that points to the new book, as REST APIs usually do.

Clear Error Responses

Without help, a missing book gives a 500 error and bad input gives a vague 400. A @RestControllerAdvice class catches exceptions from every controller and turns them into proper answers. ProblemDetail is Spring's version of the standard JSON error format (RFC 9457):

@RestControllerAdvice
public class ApiErrorHandler {

    @ExceptionHandler(BookNotFoundException.class)
    public ProblemDetail notFound(BookNotFoundException error) {
        return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, error.getMessage());
    }

    @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
    public ProblemDetail invalid(MethodArgumentNotValidException error) {
        Map<String, String> fields = new TreeMap<>();
        error.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors()
            .forEach(field -> fields.put(field.getField(), field.getDefaultMessage()));

        ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(
            HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "Some fields are invalid");
        problem.setProperty("errors", fields);
        return problem;
    }
}

Try It With curl

Start the app, then add a book:

curl -i -X POST localhost:8080/api/books \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title": "Dune", "author": "Frank Herbert", "pages": 412}'
HTTP/1.1 201
Location: /api/books/1
{"id":1,"title":"Dune","author":"Frank Herbert","pages":412}

The other endpoints:

curl localhost:8080/api/books
curl "localhost:8080/api/books?author=frank%20herbert"
curl -X PUT localhost:8080/api/books/1 -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title": "Dune", "author": "Frank Herbert", "pages": 896}'
curl -i -X DELETE localhost:8080/api/books/1

And the errors, a missing book and an empty title:

{ "detail": "No book with id 999", "status": 404, "title": "Not Found" }
{
  "detail": "Some fields are invalid",
  "status": 400,
  "title": "Bad Request",
  "errors": { "title": "must not be blank" }
}

Test It

@SpringBootTest starts the whole app with its H2 database, and MockMvc sends requests to it without a real network. JUnit and MockMvc come with the spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test starter.

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class BookControllerTest {

    @Autowired
    private MockMvc mockMvc;

    @Test
    void createsABook() throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(post("/api/books")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("""
                    {"title": "Dune", "author": "Frank Herbert", "pages": 412}
                    """))
            .andExpect(status().isCreated())
            .andExpect(header().exists("Location"))
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.title").value("Dune"));
    }

    @Test
    void answers404ForAMissingBook() throws Exception {
        mockMvc.perform(get("/api/books/999"))
            .andExpect(status().isNotFound())
            .andExpect(jsonPath("$.detail").value("No book with id 999"));
    }
}

In Spring Boot 4, @AutoConfigureMockMvc is in the org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure package. In Spring Boot 3 it was in org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.

Going Further

  • A real database. Replace H2 with PostgreSQL or MySQL: add its driver and set spring.datasource.url, username and password in application.properties. Use Flyway or Liquibase to create and change tables instead of letting Hibernate do it.
  • Paging. Return a Page from repository.findAll(Pageable) so a list of a million books doesn't come back at once.
  • Security. Add Spring Security before your API is public.
  • Turn off open-in-view. Add spring.jpa.open-in-view=false to application.properties. It's on by default, keeps a database connection for the whole request and hides lazy loading problems.

The Answer in Short

  1. Create the project at start.spring.io with Spring Web, Spring Data JPA, Validation and H2.
  2. Store data with an @Entity and a repository interface that extends JpaRepository.
  3. Put the rules in a @Service, and HTTP in a @RestController.
  4. Use records for requests and responses, with @Valid and validation rules on the request.
  5. Turn exceptions into clear ProblemDetail answers with a @RestControllerAdvice, and test the API with MockMvc.
